item.title: Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes
item.description:
Goose database migration tool supports Go functions and out-of-order changes

Goose is a database migration tool available as both a CLI and a library. It allows developers to manage database schemas by creating incremental SQL changes or Go functions.

🔍 Overview

The tool supports migrations for multiple database systems. It works against Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB, Spanner, SQLite, YDB, ClickHouse, MSSQL, and Vertica.

🧩 How it works

Goose supports specific migration formats and operational features:

  • Go migrations written as plain functions.
  • Embedded migrations.
  • Out-of-order migrations.
  • Seeding data.
  • Environment variable substitution in SQL migrations.

⚙️ Key details

The CLI includes flags for configuring migration behavior. The following table details specific flags and their functions:

Flag Description
-allow-missing Applies missing (out-of-order) migrations
-certfile File path to root CA’s certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-dir Directory with migration files (default “.”, can be set via GOOSE_MIGRATION_DIR)
-env Load environment variables from file (default .env)
-no-color Disable color output (NO_COLOR env variable supported)
-no-versioning Apply migration commands with no versioning, in file order
-s Use sequential numbering for new migrations
-ssl-cert File path to SSL certificates in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-ssl-key File path to SSL key in pem format (only supported on MySQL)
-table Migrations table name (default “goose_db_version”)
-timeout Maximum allowed duration for queries to run

🚀 Availability

Goose is available via several installation methods:

  • Go Install: go install github.com/pressly/goose/v3/cmd/goose@latest installs the binary to your $GOPATH/bin directory.
  • Homebrew: Available for macOS users.
  • Docker: A container image is available for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.
    • The container image has no shell and supports .sql migrations only.
    • The working directory is /migrations.
    • Tags include vX.Y.Z, vX.Y, vX, and latest.
    • Dockerfiles can copy the binary using: COPY --from=ghcr.io/pressly/goose:v3.30.1 /usr/local/bin/goose /usr/local/bin/goose

#Goose #Database #Go #CLI #Migrations

Source: pressly/goose

item.title: Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform
item.description:
Updates on Production-Grade Microservice Boilerplates and Wazuh Security Platform

Recent developments highlight updates regarding a production-grade microservice boilerplate and the features of the Wazuh open-source security platform.

🔍 Overview

A production-grade microservice boilerplate has been introduced, featuring tools such as GORM, Goose, Swag, Zerolog, Validator.v10, GitOps, Kubernetes, Kustomize, ArgoCD, and Istio. Additionally, Wazuh continues to serve as a free and open-source platform used for threat prevention, detection, and response across on-premises, virtualized, containerized, and cloud-based environments.

⚙️ Key details

  • The microservice boilerplate builds a production-ready containerized RESTful API server application using Go standard library net/http and the Chi router.
  • Development environments use golang:1.27-alpine (~1180 MB) and postgres:19-alpine (~440 MB), while production uses distroless/static-debian13:nonroot (~46 MB).
  • For high-traffic systems with large PostgreSQL tables, arranging fixed-width columns by decreasing alignment requirements can reduce tuple alignment padding and potentially minimize storage size, a technique called “Column Tetris”.
  • Wazuh’s architecture consists of an endpoint security agent and a management server.
  • Wazuh agents scan monitored systems for malware, rootkits, suspicious anomalies, hidden files, cloaked processes, and unregistered network listeners.
  • The Wazuh server uses a signature-based approach to intrusion detection with a regular expression engine.
  • Wazuh provides native integration with the Docker engine to monitor images, volumes, network settings, and running containers.
  • Cloud infrastructure monitoring includes integration modules for Amazon AWS, Azure, and Google Cloud.

💡 Why it matters

These tools help organizations build robust containerized RESTful APIs with automated GitOps deployment via ArgoCD, while maintaining comprehensive security, threat detection, and regulatory compliance with standards such as PCI DSS, GPG13, and GDPR using Wazuh.

#Microservices #Go #Kubernetes #Security #Wazuh

Source: learning-cloud-native-go/myapp Source: dokku/dokku Source: wazuh/wazuh

item.title: Go client released for Qdrant vector search engine
item.description:
Go client released for Qdrant vector search engine

The Go client for the Qdrant vector search engine has been released, making it easier for developers to integrate vector search capabilities into their Go applications. Internally, the high-level client uses a low-level gRPC client to interact with Qdrant, abstracting away the complexity of direct API calls. The client supports secure communication with TLS 1.3 as the minimum required version when UseTLS is enabled.

📦 Availability

The client can be installed using the Go package manager:

  • go get -u github.com/qdrant/go-client

🔐 Security

  • Uses TLS 1.3 as the minimum security version when UseTLS: true is set

🧩 Architecture

  • High-level client provides simplified API for common operations
  • Low-level gRPC client handles direct communication with Qdrant server

💡 Why it matters

This release enables Go developers to leverage Qdrant’s vector search capabilities without implementing low-level networking code, accelerating the development of AI and machine learning applications that require semantic search functionality.

#Go #Qdrant #VectorSearch #gRPC #TLS #AI

Source: qdrant/go-client

item.title: Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents
item.description:
Update on Deja-Vu: Local Memory and Cross-Agent Handoff for 48 Coding Agents

Deja-vu (deja) has received new updates providing local memory, session search, and cross-agent handoff across 48 coding agents including Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, and Hermes.

🔍 Overview

  • Supports 48 coding agents that already save every session to disk.
  • Built as a single Go binary featuring 7 hooks and MCP.
  • Indexes all session data locally with zero LLM calls, achieving a 0.7 ms in-process lookup and a ~4% index footprint.
  • Achieves a recall of 97.2% R@5 on LongMemEval-S.

🧩 Features and Commands

  • Interactive terminal search: Running deja with no arguments opens a search across every agent’s history, prioritizing sessions behind uncommitted changes and recent work in the current project.
  • Navigation: Use up and down arrows to pick a session, enter to open at the match, forward slash to search inside a session, square brackets to jump between turns, and Control-s to toggle date or relevance sort (deja search --sort date).
  • Filtering: Filter by agent (e.g., codex:), time (today, yesterday, week, month), or project (in:<project>).
  • Session management: Press r to reopen a session in its native agent, or o to continue it in another agent with its goal, decisions, and open work.
  • Recover deleted chats: Tab switches between the current project, all projects, and Deleted sessions.
  • Command-line tools:
    • deja "jwt refresh token": Lexical plus structural search across all 48 agent stores.
    • deja handoff --to codex: Continue the active session’s goal and state in another agent.
    • deja restore internal/auth/jwt.go: Recover code an agent overwrote before git commit.
    • deja blame internal/auth/jwt.go:42: Trace which agent session wrote or replaced a line.
    • deja audit: Check retention risk, purged chats, and index health across all 48 stores.

⚙️ Performance Benchmarks

  • Recall: 97.2% LongMemEval-S (compared to MemPalace at 96.6% and agentmemory at 95.2%).
  • Token usage: Uses half the tokens of agentmemory on a task the machine had already solved.
  • Speed: Indexing and lookup take 13.6 seconds and 0.7 ms lookup across 19,195 sessions (next of 7 tools took 72 seconds).

🚀 Availability

  • Node.js / npm: npx @vshulcz/deja-vu install --auto (1-step cross-platform install and wire installed agents).
  • Shell script: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/vshulcz/deja-vu/main/install.sh | sh && deja install --auto.
  • Homebrew: brew install deja-vu && deja install --auto.

#AIagents #ClaudeCode #Go #DeveloperTools #Memory

Source: vshulcz/deja-vu

item.title: Chroma v3 Released with Go iter.Seq Support
item.description:
Chroma v3 Released with Go iter.Seq Support

Chroma v3 has been released as a new alpha version, bringing significant changes to its Go implementation and module path.

🔍 Overview

Chroma takes source code and other structured text and converts it into syntax highlighted HTML, ANSI-coloured text, and other formats. It is based heavily on Pygments and includes translators for Pygments lexers and styles.

⚙️ Key details

  • Replaces the custom Iterator type with Go’s built-in iter.Seq[Token]
  • Removes the EOF sentinel
  • Bumps the module path to github.com/alecthomas/chroma/v3

🧩 How it works

  • Lexers convert source text into a stream of tokens
  • Styles specify how token types are mapped to colours
  • Formatters convert tokens and styles into formatted output

🚀 Availability

  • See the v3.0.0-alpha.1 release for migration details
  • Try out various languages and styles on the Chroma Playground
  • An authoritative list of languages and styles can be displayed with chroma --list

#Chroma #Go #Pygments #SyntaxHighlighting

Source: alecthomas/chroma

item.title: Webframe: Go Tool for Running Web Pages as Programs
item.description:
Webframe: Go Tool for Running Web Pages as Programs

Jeff Lindsay released webframe, a Go project that lets you run a web page like a program. It executes the page in a hidden headless web view, streaming console.log() output to standard output and routing exceptions to standard error.

🔍 Overview

  • Runs any URL or local file as a program.
  • Outputs JavaScript console.log() to stdout.
  • Sends JavaScript exceptions to stderr.
  • Compared to the author’s own shot‑scraper tool, webframe is a much smaller package and does not rely on Playwright.

🧩 How it works

  • Implemented in Go, built on the glaze library.
  • glaze accesses the system‑installed browser engine, so webframe does not bundle its own engine.
  • Supported system browsers:
    Operating System System Browser
    macOS WKWebView
    Linux WebKitGTK
    Windows WebView2

⚙️ Key details

  • Project URL: https://github.com/tractordev/webframe
  • Designed to run headlessly; the browser view is hidden.
  • Provides a lightweight alternative for tasks that traditionally use larger frameworks such as Playwright.

🚀 Evaluation as a sandboxing tool

  • Claude Opus 5.5 was prompted to explore the repository, build exploratory prototypes, and assess webframe’s suitability as a sandboxing environment.
  • The prompt asked the model to “put it through its paces” and evaluate security‑related aspects, though specific outcomes are not detailed in the source.

📡 Evaluation as a scraping tool

  • The same Claude Opus 5.5 prompt also asked the model to evaluate webframe for scraping web pages using patterns similar to the shot‑scraper JavaScript command (see simonw/shot‑scraper on GitHub).
  • The evaluation aimed to compare webframe’s scraping capabilities against the existing shot‑scraper approach, focusing on its minimal footprint and lack of Playwright dependency.

#webframe #Go #WebScraping #Sandboxing

Source: Research: webframe: evaluated as a scraper and a sandbox

item.title: AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol using policy network and tree search
item.description:
AlphaGo defeats Lee Sedol using policy network and tree search

On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time.

🔍 Overview

  • Move 37 in game two of the five‑game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.
  • The move had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player.
  • AlphaGo’s choice was driven by its search machinery, not by the “intuitive” policy network alone.

🧩 How AlphaGo works

  • AlphaGo is made up of two systems.
  • The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play.
  • The search component explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.
  • As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree, updating it and eventually synthesizing the information to decide which move to make.

♟️ Comparison to Deep Blue

  • When Deep Blue defeated then‑reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard‑coded by humans.
  • Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years.

🧠 Cognitive analogy

  • A well‑known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 (fast, gut‑level) and System 2 (slow, deliberative).
  • AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split: its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow.

🤖 Contrast with large language models

  • A large language model picks the next token, over and over.
  • Researchers have added chain‑of‑thought prompting so models can generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning.
  • The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next‑token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.
  • However, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state; there is no open ledger of hypotheses, confidence, or evidence.
  • Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs.
  • Research has shown that bots often concoct chain‑of‑thought explanations after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.
  • By contrast, AlphaGo’s game tree provides an explicit, inspectable record of the variations it considered.

📊 Key facts

  • AlphaGo won 4‑1 against Lee Sedol.
  • Move 37 had a ≈1/10,000 chance of being chosen by a human expert.
  • Deep Blue evaluated 200 million positions per second.
  • Go’s outcome space is so large that exhaustive computation would take billions of years on a supercomputer.
  • AlphaGo’s architecture combines a policy network with tree search and a game‑tree data structure.

#AlphaGo #Go #AI #MachineLearning #DeepLearning

Source: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
